messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Six months ago, Frank’s sedan was T-boned at a busy intersection, rolling onto its roof while the guardrail groaned and the windshield spider-webbed. When he finally crawled from the twisted door, the sharp tang of ruptured coolant mixed with the acrid stench of scorched brakes, a sensory collision that immediately hijacked his nervous system. His heart hammered against his ribs, and the violent jolt of that impact left him permanently jumpy, so that even ordinary car horns now spiked his pulse into a frantic, breathless reaction. The memory of the crash refused to settle into a coherent narrative; whenever he tried to explain what happened to his son, he would lose the thread, and the fragmented audio of snapping seatbelts and grinding metal would echo in his head as if it belonged to someone else. This inability to piece the event together convinced Frank that he was fundamentally weak, that a competent military medic would never have misjudged that stop sign. That harsh self-judgment took root quickly, and he became convinced he could not trust his own judgment anymore. Determined to prevent another failure, Frank began constantly monitoring his own thoughts for any sign of mental unraveling. He started suppressing any memory of the collision, trying hard not to think about the trauma, which only forced the fragmented recollections deeper, making them feel even more alien and detached from his own life. Because he viewed himself as weak and blamed himself for the crash, he avoided driving and would not even ride as a passenger in a vehicle. This avoidance quickly bred profound physical reactivity; the mere thought of a steering wheel triggered a cold sweat and a trembling that made him feel utterly jumpy. The physical panic then acted as a beacon, pulling his attention straight back to the smell of alcohol on a colleague’s breath or the sight of dented fenders on parked cars, convincing him that danger was everywhere. When he tried to push the triggers away, the suppressed memories surfaced with greater auditory clarity, and these loud, uncontrollable flashbacks reinforced his belief that he was losing control and could never be sure of his own instincts. The more he doubted his own competence, the more his body prepared for catastrophe, which in turn made ordinary noises trigger a violent startle response, ensuring that every reminder of the crash felt overwhelmingly potent. Now stationed at the community VA clinic as a senior military medic, Frank finds himself trapped in this tightening loop. Last Tuesday, a supply delivery truck idled outside his office window, its diesel fumes drifting through the cracked pane. The burnt smell instantly triggered a full-body tremor, which flooded his mind with the auditory recall of the original impact, stripping the event of any sense of ownership and leaving it feeling entirely alien. His immediate thought monitoring flagged the panic as a sign of impending collapse, driving him to suppress the memory again, which only deepened his conviction that he was too broken to care for patients. He has not driven or ridden in a car since the accident, isolating himself from the road and abandoning his favorite weekend walks through the downtown district. He finally scheduled this intake because the suppression is no longer holding, and the constant hypervigilance has left him exhausted and certain that he is losing his mind. He is most afraid of another collision, but he desperately hopes the treatment might finally help him trust his own hands again.
